answer.summary: Immich-style pipeline, traced from the upload request. Each background stage is started by the previous job finishing with Success or Skipped: JobService.onJobRun calls onDone, which switches on the completed job name and queues the next job(s). Starting points: AssetMediaService.uploadAsset queues AssetExtractMetadata directly with source 'upload'. Metadata extraction emits AssetMetadataExtracted, and the StorageTemplate listener queues StorageTemplateMigrationSingle. Its onDone queues AssetGenerateThumbnails. Thumbnail onDone fans out to SmartSearch (CLIP embedding, which enables natural-language search), AssetDetectFaces (grouping under people) and Ocr. SmartSearch onDone (source upload) queues AssetDetectDuplicates, which runs the near-duplicate comparison. The face branch runs in parallel: DetectFaces queues FacialRecognition per new face, and handleRecognizeFaces assigns the person. A failed or hidden step stops the chain.

Each queued job runs through JobService.onJobRun, and when it returns Success/Skipped, JobService.onDone queues the next stage. MetadataService.handleMetadataExtraction emits AssetMetadataExtracted, which StorageTemplateService.onAssetMetadataExtracted turns into StorageTemplateMigrationSingle. Metadata extraction emits AssetMetadataExtracted, which a StorageTemplateService listener turns into StorageTemplateMigrationSingle. When that job finishes (Success or Skipped), JobService.onDone queues AssetGenerateThumbnails. When thumbnails finish, JobService.onDone queues SmartSearch (CLIP embedding, making the photo searchable in natural language), AssetDetectFaces and Ocr together. For a public share link, the original is served only if these checks pass, in order. (1) AuthGuard.canActivate calls AuthService.authenticate, which calls validate. That resolves the share key (or slug) through validateSharedLinkKey or validateSharedLinkSlug, which look up the link via SharedLinkRepository.getByKey or getBySlug. The lookup (authBuilder) requires the link to have an owner user, and it must be an individual link or an album link whose album is not deleted. isValidSharedLink then rejects links that are missing or expired. (2) authenticate rejects shared auth on non-shared routes; the route is marked sharedLink:true, so this passes. (3) downloadAsset passes the id to AssetMediaService.downloadOriginal, which calls requireAccess with AssetDownload. checkSharedLinkAccess returns nothing unless the link has allowDownload. Otherwise AssetAccess.checkSharedLinkAccess keeps only non-deleted assets that are in the link's shared-link asset list or in its non-deleted album, including a live photo's video companion. If any requested id is missing from the allowed set, requireAccess throws BadRequest. (4) getForOriginal loads the path; for shared visitors isEditedOnly forces the edited file when one exists. Missing assets throw. (5) sendFile checks the file is readable (R_OK) before streaming; any failure becomes NotFound. Note: the link password is selected but not checked anywhere on this path, which I did not trace further.

answer.summary: A share-link visitor's original-file request passes these checks in order. (1) AuthGuard resolves the share key or slug and validates it: the key or slug must match a link whose owner user exists, whose album (if any) is not deleted, and which has not expired. (2) AuthService.authenticate requires the route to be marked sharedLink. (3) requireAccess asks whether AssetDownload is allowed: the link needs allowDownload, and the asset must be non-deleted and reachable through the link directly or through its non-deleted album (including live-photo video). (4) downloadOriginal fetches the path, preferring the edited full-size file because isEditedOnly is true for share-link auth. (5) sendFile checks the file is readable (R_OK) and streams it, returning 404 on error. Caveat: the password field is loaded but I did not see it checked in this path.

answer.summary: Trash is a soft delete: AssetService.deleteAll sets deletedAt and status Trashed. Nightly, QueueService.handleNightlyJobs queues AssetDeleteCheck (default 00:00, only if nightlyTasks.databaseCleanup is on). AssetService.handleAssetDeletionCheck then queues AssetDelete {deleteOnDisk: true} for every asset with deletedAt older than trash.days (default 30; 0 if trash is disabled). handleAssetDeletion handles the stack, removes the row, decrements quota, emits AssetDelete, and queues FileDelete. Its files are the derived previews/thumbnails always, and the original and sidecar only when deleteOnDisk is set and the asset is not offline. The live-photo partner (the motion video, normally Hidden) is not trashed with the still. It is purged in the same way only once no other still references it (getLivePhotoCount, checked after the still's row is removed). Ordered flow: the schedule (QueueService.onConfigInit/onConfigUpdate → asNightlyTasksCron → handleNightlyJobs), then the check job, the AssetDelete job, the file job, and the motion partner handling.

answer.summary: Scheduling: on config init/update, QueueService schedules a NightlyJobs cron (asNightlyTasksCron, default startTime 00:00, databaseCleanup on by default), and handleNightlyJobs queues AssetDeleteCheck. AssetService.handleAssetDeletionCheck computes cutoff = now − trash.days (default 30; 0 if trash disabled), streams every asset with deletedAt <= cutoff, and queues an AssetDelete job per asset with deleteOnDisk=true. AssetService.handleAssetDeletion then loads the asset, fixes its stack, deletes its DB row (asset_file rows cascade), adjusts user quota for non-library assets, and emits AssetDelete (websocket notification). For the live-photo partner: if livePhotoVideoId is set and no other asset still references the motion video (getLivePhotoCount === 0), it queues AssetDelete for the motion video with the same deleteOnDisk; the motion video is a Hidden asset that is never trashed on its own, so this cascade is its only removal path. A manual empty (TrashService.empty → status Deleted → AssetEmptyTrash job → handleEmptyTrash) converges on the same AssetDelete path. Caveats: the still and its motion video are deleted in separate jobs, so a crash between them can leave the motion video behind until a later run.

QueueService.handleNightlyJobs queues AssetDeleteCheck, which AssetService.handleAssetDeletionCheck runs against assets with deletedAt before the cutoff. answer.summary: Immich's retention is `config.trash.days` (default 30, enabled by default). Trashing via AssetService.deleteAll only sets status=Trashed and deletedAt on the photo. A nightly cron (QueueService, default 00:00, gated by databaseCleanup) enqueues AssetDeleteCheck. AssetService.handleAssetDeletionCheck streams assets with deletedAt <= now - days and queues AssetDelete(deleteOnDisk=true) for each. AssetService.handleAssetDeletion then runs: loads the asset, fixes any stack, removes the DB row, decrements user quota, emits AssetDelete, and handles the live-photo partner. The partner (motion video, a separate hidden asset) is queued for AssetDelete only if no other asset still references it after the photo row is removed; its own handleAssetDeletion then runs the same way. Finally, a FileDelete job unlinks the derivative files (thumbnail, preview, fullsize, edits, encoded video) and, because deleteOnDisk is true, also the sidecar and the original file. Each recipient gets at most one "New media" email per burst because every album-add emits an AlbumUpdate event that, for each recipient, removes the pending NotifyAlbumUpdate job keyed `${albumId}/${recipientId}` and re-queues it with a fresh 5-minute delay. The job is a debounce: the email is sent once, 5 minutes after the last addition, and only one job per (album, recipient) exists at a time. answer.summary: Most likely root cause (code-level; not reproduced with ffmpeg/QSV): HLS variants on QSV are encoded in ICQ mode, not a capped bitrate mode. With cqMode=auto (the default), QsvSwDecodeConfig.useCQP() is false, so getBitrateOptions emits `-global_quality:v <crf>` plus `-maxrate`/`-bufsize`. ICQ is quality-targeted, and I believe the QSV driver does not enforce maxrate in that mode, so 2-second segments can far exceed the variant's nominal bitrate. generateMainPlaylist still advertises BANDWIDTH = bitrate×1.35, so on a 40 Mbit WAN the client picks a variant whose real segments take longer than 2s to download, causing periodic stalls. LAN has enough headroom to hide this. The rising "lead" shows the producer is ahead of the viewer, which fits. I checked the backpressure path (applyBackpressure/pauseTranscode) and ruled it out: it pauses only once 30+ segments are already on disk and resumes below 15, so it cannot starve the player. The fix is to use a capped VBR-style rate control for HLS on QSV (not ICQ) or otherwise make the advertised BANDWIDTH match what is actually produced; the ICQ/maxrate choice is the part to verify on hardware.

It computes lead = lastCompletedSegment − lastClientRequestedSegment and SIGSTOPs ffmpeg above 30 segments (HLS_BACKPRESSURE_PAUSE_SEGMENTS), then SIGCONTs below 15 (HLS_BACKPRESSURE_RESUME_SEGMENTS). A stall would need a request for a segment not yet produced, which the code only sees on a forward seek (restart path) or a variant switch (restart path), or a delay in transfer rather than production. Those restart paths in onSegmentRequest/startTranscode are the next candidates. The WAN-only trigger is most likely client-side ABR or request timing, which the server cannot see directly. Confidence is moderate-to-low, and the mechanism needs a reproduction with debug logs showing HlsSegmentRequest and restart events during a stall.

answer.summary: Root cause: the birth date response is formatted in the server's local time zone, but the Date it is built from is UTC midnight, so west-of-UTC servers show the previous day. The stored value is written as a plain 'YYYY-MM-DD' string and is not shifted. On read, the DB driver (postgres.js, per the package.json and my recollection of its default `date` parser, which I could not confirm because node_modules and the sql-tools package are not in this checkout) turns the `date` column into `new Date('YYYY-MM-DD')`, which is UTC midnight. `isoDateToDate.encode` then calls `DateTime.fromJSDate(date).toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd')` without a UTC zone, so UTC midnight becomes the previous calendar day in any negative-offset local zone. Its own decode (`new Date(isoString)`) is UTC, so the codec is internally inconsistent. The fix is to format in UTC (`DateTime.fromJSDate(date, { zone: 'utc' })`), which matches how user-methods.ts already treats dates. If the web client re-submits the shifted value on later saves, that would explain why the user sees it "keep changing"; I did not verify the client side.
